mcqs.question: Why does the deep-dive phase typically get more time and more scoring weight than the high-level design phase?
options: It's where you show judgment on a component's trade-offs under scrutiny, not just breadth of recall
It's simply the last phase before wrap-up, so any remaining time defaults to it
Interviewers use it mainly to test whiteboard tool proficiency
It's the only phase where non-functional requirements are allowed to be discussed
mcqs.explanation: Deep dive is weighted heavily because depth under scrutiny — defending a trade-off, handling a follow-up — is a much stronger signal than a correct-looking high-level diagram. It isn't leftover time, isn't about tool proficiency, and non-functional requirements matter throughout the interview, not just in one phase.

mcqs.question: A candidate immediately sketches a database schema and hash-function design for "design a URL shortener" without asking any questions. What's the main risk?
options: The interviewer will assume the candidate doesn't understand hash functions
The design may solve the wrong problem — for example, over-engineering for writes when the real workload is read-heavy
Whiteboard diagrams are only accepted after the ten-minute mark
URL shorteners cannot be designed without a load balancer
mcqs.explanation: Skipping requirements risks solving a problem the interviewer never asked about — over- or under-building for the actual read/write ratio, scale, or feature set. It has nothing to do with hash-function knowledge, a whiteboard timing rule, or a hard requirement for a load balancer.

mcqs.question: What most reliably distinguishes a candidate who sounds scripted from one who's comfortably using the same framework?
options: The scripted candidate uses a whiteboard while the other uses a shared doc
The scripted candidate finishes several minutes faster
The scripted candidate announces each phase by name; the other lets transitions emerge from the conversation
The scripted candidate skips the wrap-up phase entirely
mcqs.explanation: Explicitly narrating the framework ("Now I will move to the estimation phase") is what reads as recital; the same coverage delivered as natural transitions reads as fluency. Tool choice, raw speed, and skipping wrap-up aren't the actual signal here.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't drawing a detailed architecture quickly, before requirements are clarified, read as a sign of strength to most interviewers?
options: Fast drawing violates most companies' interview policies
It uses up whiteboard space needed later for the deep dive
Interviewers dock points for speed regardless of content
Without requirements, the interviewer can't tell if the design fits the problem, and follow-ups about unasked scale or features become moot
mcqs.explanation: Confidence that matters is fit-to-requirements, not speed of the first sketch. There's no such policy, whiteboard space isn't the real constraint, and interviewers don't penalize raw speed — they penalize a design that turns out not to match the actual requirements.
